sentences.text: The known remains include a partial skull featuring a long, narrow snout that resembles the false gharial, suggesting a diet focused on fish.
In this animal, the single preserved functional tooth located in the front of the upper jaw angled slightly outward rather than pointing straight down.
This species was pseudoheterodont, a condition where the front teeth varied greatly in size while the rear teeth remained relatively uniform.
Unlike other crocodiles where the fifth upper tooth is the largest, the fourth tooth in the front section was the biggest in Harpacochampsa.
The genus name combines Greek words for 'to seize' and 'crocodile,' highlighting the specialized nature of these front teeth.
Scientists Megirian, Murray, and Willis first described this genus in the year 1991.
The fossils were uncovered at the Bullock Creek site located within the Northern Territory of Australia.
This extinct crocodilian genus is known from the Cañada Bullock lagerstätte, a famous fossil deposit in the Northern Territory.
Its elongated snout indicates that Harpacochampsa was a piscivore, or fish-eater, during its life.
While it likely ate fish and turtles, its sturdy build suggests it might have also hunted medium-sized mammals.
Harpachochampsa is classified as a reptile.
It belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.
The species is placed within the family Crocodylidae.
Its placement in the subfamily Mekosuchinae is uncertain and often marked with question marks.
Some experts doubt this subfamily assignment because Harpacochampsa might be the only known mekosuchine with such a long, thin snout.
This animal lived during the Early Miocene epoch.
Its time range spans from the Langhian to the Serravallian stages, occurring between 15.98 and 11.63 million years ago.
It is debated whether Harpacochampsa belongs to the Mekosuchinae, is a basal crocodyloid, or is a type of gavialid.
The classification of Harpacochampsa within Mekosuchinae has been questioned by various authors, making its exact position controversial.
Ristevski et al. (2021) recovered Harpacochampsa as one of the basalmost crocodyloids, neither a mekosuchine nor a gavialoid.
